title: Train a Simple Model (Lab)
summary: Groups build a training set of safe, non-personal examples, train a classifier, test it on held-back examples, and check how their choices shaped the model.
objectives: Train a simple classifier on non-personal examples (objects/drawings/sounds) and test it on new examples.
Explain how the training examples shaped what the model learned.
Run a basic risk and data-safety check on the training set.

body: Today you become a model trainer. You choose the examples, and the examples decide what your model learns - so choose wisely and keep them safe.

terms.definition: The examples the model learns from.
New examples, held back, used to check the model.
The pattern the system builds from the training data.
A model that sorts examples into categories.
Use only non-personal examples - never faces, voices or names.

sections.heading: Train, then test
body: First you show the model many labelled [[training data]] examples. It finds the pattern and builds a [[model]].
Then you test it on new examples it has never seen. If it still gets them right, it really learned. If not, it only memorised.

sections.heading: Your examples shape the model
body: If all your apple pictures are red, the model learns 'red', not 'apple', and fails on a green one. Variety and fairness matter, not just how many.
**Golden rule:** only non-personal examples. No faces, no voices, no names ever go into a training set.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Build a training set of safe, non-personal examples, train a model, then test it on new examples and check your data is safe.
items: Pick two categories of non-personal items.
Collect and label 8-10 training examples each.
Test the held-back examples and log the results.
Complete the data-safety and risk check.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which testing example fooled the model, and why?
How did your choice of examples change what it learned?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write how your training examples shaped the model.
Write one data-safety rule you followed today.

worksheet.title: Week 2 Lab worksheet - Train a Simple Model

questions.prompt: Put the lab steps in the order that gives a fair test of the model.

items.text: Pick two categories of non-personal items.
Collect and label 8-10 examples of each category.
Hide 3 examples of each category so the model will never see them.
Train the model using the remaining examples only.
Run the hidden examples through the model and log the results.

feedback.correct: The testing examples have to be set aside before training, or the model has already seen them and the test proves nothing.
feedback.incorrect: Check where the hiding step sits: examples must be held back before training, otherwise you are testing the model on work it already memorised.

questions.prompt: A group trained a 'cup' classifier. Every cup in their training examples was white. When they tested a red cup that had been held back, the model said 'not a cup'. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The model learned 'white' as well as 'cup', because every training example shared that colour.
The model simply did not have enough training examples.
The red cup was a testing example, and models always get testing examples wrong.
The model memorised the red cup during training and got confused.

feedback.correct: When every example shares a feature, the model learns that feature too - this is the red-cup version of the red-apple problem.
feedback.incorrect: More examples of the same white cups would not help, and the red cup was never in training; the problem is that the training examples had no variety in colour.

questions.prompt: A group wants to find out whether their model really learned 'circle' or only memorised their pictures. Select every action that would help them find out.

options.text: Test it on circles that were held back and never used in training.
Include circles of different sizes and colours among the testing examples.
Write down the prediction for each example before running it through the model.
Test it again using the same pictures it was trained on.
Add more copies of the training pictures to the testing set.
Judge the model by how quickly it gives each answer.

feedback.correct: Unseen and varied examples, with your prediction written first, is what turns a test into real evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Anything the model has already seen will be answered correctly whether it learned or memorised, and speed says nothing about what it learned.

questions.prompt: True or false: a model that gets every training example right but fails almost every held-back example has learned its categories well.

feedback.correct: Correct - getting the training examples right only shows it memorised them; real learning shows up on examples it has never seen.
feedback.incorrect: Scoring well on the examples it was trained on is easy; because it fails the held-back examples, this model memorised rather than learned.

questions.prompt: Complete the lab's rules about safe data and a fair check.
questions.stem: Training examples must be non-{{1}}, which means no faces, voices or names. The examples you hide are called {{2}} data, and they are a fair check only because the model never saw them during {{3}}.

feedback.correct: Safe data and a clean split between training and testing are the two things that make your log trustworthy.
feedback.incorrect: The golden rule is non-personal examples only, and the held-back set is the testing data - it works as a check because it stayed out of training.

formative.targets: Deepens 'recognises the difference between rule-based and learning systems' by building a learning system and seeing how data shapes it
formative.check: Training-and-testing log with results and an explanation of how the data shaped the model
formative.successCriteria: Trains and tests a model on separate example sets and explains how the training examples changed what it learned.
formative.evidence: Completed training/testing log plus the data-safety and risk check.
